title: A Sunday on La Grande Jatte
why: Seurat built this huge scene of Parisians at leisure from tiny dots of pure colour, trusting your eye to blend them. It took him about two years. The stiff, almost frozen figures make an ordinary Sunday feel strange and timeless, and the technique, pointillism, influenced a generation of painters.

title: The Bedroom
why: Van Gogh painted his room in Arles three times; this is the second version. He wanted it to feel restful, using flat, bright colour and simple shapes, yet the tilted walls and floor give it a restless energy. It is one of the most intimate self-portraits ever made without a face in it.

title: Self-Portrait
why: Painted in Paris in 1887, when Van Gogh was absorbing the Impressionists and Seurat. The short, rhythmic strokes and complementary colours show him finding the style that made him famous. He painted himself often partly because he could not afford models.

title: Paris Street; Rainy Day
why: Caillebotte captured the new, wide boulevards of a Paris rebuilt by Baron Haussmann. Everyone is close together yet nobody connects, an early picture of modern city loneliness. The precise, almost photographic finish set him apart from his Impressionist friends.

title: The Child's Bath
why: Cassatt was one of very few women in the Impressionist circle, and she made the everyday care of children a serious subject for art. The flattened patterns and high viewpoint show the influence of Japanese prints. It is tender without being sentimental.

title: Stacks of Wheat (End of Summer)
why: Monet painted these ordinary stacks of grain dozens of times in different seasons and light. The subject hardly matters; the point is how light and air change everything we see. The series pushed painting a step closer to abstraction.

title: Water Lilies
why: In his garden at Giverny, Monet spent nearly thirty years painting his lily pond. There is no horizon and no edge, just water, reflection and sky folding into each other. Later abstract painters looked back to these as a starting point.

title: Arrival of the Normandy Train, Gare Saint-Lazare
why: Monet turned a busy railway station into a study of steam, smoke and light. Trains stood for speed and the modern age, and painting them was a statement that modern life deserved art. The glass roof frames the whole scene like a stage.

title: At the Moulin Rouge
why: Toulouse-Lautrec knew the Paris nightclubs from the inside and painted their regulars. The green-lit face cut off at the right edge is startling and cinematic. It shows nightlife as glamorous and slightly sad at the same time.

title: Two Sisters (On the Terrace)
why: Renoir painted a young woman and a little girl on a terrace above the Seine, softened by feathery brushwork. The models were not in fact sisters. It is one of the clearest examples of his love of warm colour, light and simple pleasure.

title: Acrobats at the Cirque Fernando
why: Two young circus performers, Francisca and Angelina Wartenberg, take a bow among the oranges thrown by the crowd. Renoir puts us down in the ring with them rather than in the audience. The painting celebrates working entertainers rather than wealthy sitters.

title: The Herring Net
why: Homer spent two years living in a fishing village on the English coast, then settled on the coast of Maine. Here two fishermen haul in a catch in a heavy sea. It is a quiet tribute to dangerous, unglamorous work and people facing nature together.

title: Mrs. George Swinton
why: Sargent was the most fashionable portrait painter of his day, and this is a show of pure skill. The shimmering dress is made from loose, quick strokes that only make sense from a distance. It tells you a lot about wealth and display in the 1890s.

title: The Assumption of the Virgin
why: This was El Greco's first major commission after he arrived in Spain from Greece via Italy. The long, flame-like figures and vivid colour were unusual then and later fascinated modern artists. It shows how one painter blended Byzantine, Venetian and Spanish traditions.

title: The Basket of Apples
why: The table tilts, the edges do not line up, and the bottle leans. Cézanne showed objects from slightly different angles at once. That idea opened the door to Cubism and much of twentieth-century art.

title: Madame Cézanne in a Yellow Chair
why: Hortense Fiquet sat for Cézanne more than forty times. She is often described as expressionless, but he was more interested in structure and form than in mood. The painting treats a person with the same steady attention as a mountain or an apple.

title: Under the Wave off Kanagawa (The Great Wave)
why: Hokusai's woodblock print shows fishing boats under a huge wave with Mount Fuji small in the distance. Prints like this were cheap and made in thousands of copies. When they reached Europe they changed how Western artists thought about composition and colour.

title: The Song of the Lark
why: A young peasant woman stops on her way to work at sunrise to listen to a bird. Breton painted rural life with dignity at a time when many people were leaving the land. It became one of the most popular paintings in America in the early twentieth century.

title: The Millinery Shop
why: Degas spent years on this picture of a woman, perhaps a milliner, among hats. Her face is half hidden, and the hats get more attention than she does. It hints at the unseen labour behind fashion in Paris.

title: Woman at Her Toilette
why: Morisot was a founding member of the Impressionists and showed in nearly all their exhibitions. Her brushwork here is so free that the picture almost dissolves. She painted the private spaces of women's lives, which male painters rarely saw.

title: No te aha oe riri (Why Are You Angry?)
why: Gauguin painted this in Tahiti. The flat areas of rich colour influenced modern art deeply. It is also worth looking at critically: his romantic image of the Pacific says as much about European fantasies of the 'exotic' as about the people he painted.

title: Old Man with a Gold Chain
why: A young Rembrandt painted this character study rather than a commissioned portrait. The light falls on the face and the glinting chain while the rest sinks into shadow. Studies like this taught him the psychological depth his later portraits are famous for.

title: Young Woman at an Open Half-Door
why: Made in Rembrandt's workshop, this shows a girl leaning on a Dutch half-door, half in light and half in shadow. Workshops often produced paintings in the master's style. It raises good questions about authorship and what 'a Rembrandt' really means.

title: Interrupted Reading
why: Corot is best known for misty landscapes, but late in life he painted thoughtful figures like this. The woman has looked up from her book, lost in thought. It captures an inner moment rather than an action.

title: Improvisation No. 30 (Cannons)
why: Kandinsky was one of the first painters to move fully towards abstraction. Painted in 1913, on the eve of the First World War, it includes the shapes of cannons firing among colours. He believed colour and form could work on us like music.

title: Cliff Walk at Pourville
why: Two figures stand on a windy clifftop above the Normandy sea. Monet uses quick, broken strokes to make grass, wind and light feel alive. It is a small, joyful painting of a moment outdoors.

title: The Poet's Garden
why: Van Gogh painted this public garden in Arles to decorate the room where he hoped Gauguin would stay. He imagined it as the kind of garden a poet would love. The thick yellows and greens show his happiest, most hopeful period.

title: Jesus Mocked by the Soldiers
why: Manet, known for modern Paris scenes, tackled a religious subject here and was criticised for it. His Christ looks like an ordinary, exhausted man rather than an idealised figure. It shows him questioning the traditions of grand history painting.

title: The Bay of Marseille, Seen from L'Estaque
why: Cézanne painted this view many times. He built the landscape out of solid blocks of colour, making sea, roofs and hills feel almost architectural. Young painters like Braque later went to L'Estaque because of him.

title: Fishing Boats with Hucksters Bargaining for Fish
why: Turner was obsessed with weather, sea and light. Here boats pitch in rough water as traders haggle over a catch. His loose, atmospheric style looked unfinished to many critics, but it pointed towards Impressionism.

title: The Two Disciples at the Tomb
why: Henry Ossawa Tanner was the first African American painter to gain international fame, and he worked mostly in Paris. This painting won a major prize at the Art Institute in 1906. The light falling on the two faces turns a Bible story into a moment of quiet shock and wonder.

title: Mère Grégoire
why: Courbet led the Realist movement, which insisted on painting ordinary people as they really were. Here a café owner sits at her counter. She is solid, shrewd and unidealised, a deliberate contrast to the polished goddesses of academic art.

title: Yellow Dancers (In the Wings)
why: Degas painted ballet dancers again and again, often off stage rather than performing. These dancers wait in the wings, adjusting straps and stretching. The unusual angle feels like a snapshot, influenced by photography.

title: The Rock of Hautepierre
why: Courbet grew up in the Jura region of France and painted its cliffs and rivers often. He sometimes used a palette knife to build up rock-like texture. It is landscape painted with weight and physical presence.

title: Saint George and the Dragon
why: Bernat Martorell was a leading painter in fifteenth-century Catalonia, where Saint George is the patron saint. The gold, detailed armour and calm princess are typical of the International Gothic style. It is a reminder of how much art served faith and civic pride.

title: Nocturne: Blue and Gold, Southampton Water
why: Whistler gave his paintings musical titles to suggest that art should be about mood and harmony, not storytelling. This is mostly blue haze with a few lights. His 'nocturnes' famously led to a libel trial with the critic John Ruskin.

title: Kanbara: Evening Snow
why: From Hiroshige's series on the fifty-three stations of the Tōkaidō road between Edo and Kyoto. Travellers trudge through deep snow in near silence. Its calm mood made it one of the best-loved Japanese prints.

title: Sudden Shower over Shin-Ōhashi Bridge
why: Hiroshige shows people hurrying across a bridge as a downpour hits, with the rain drawn as fine dark lines. Van Gogh admired it so much he painted his own copy. It is a lesson in how to show weather and movement simply.

title: Plum Garden at Kameido
why: A plum tree's branch fills the foreground while visitors look small behind it. Hiroshige's bold cropping was radical. Van Gogh copied this print too, and it shaped how European artists framed their scenes.

title: After the Bullfight
why: An early Cassatt, painted in Seville before she joined the Impressionists. A picador rests and smokes after the fight. It shows her strong figure painting and her interest in Spanish art.

title: Cattle at Rest on a Hillside in the Alps
why: Rosa Bonheur was the most famous woman painter of the nineteenth century and specialised in animals. She received official permission to wear trousers so she could work at markets and fairs. She studied anatomy closely, and it shows.

title: Veranda Post (Òpó Ògògá)
why: Olowe of Ise was one of the great Yoruba sculptors of the early twentieth century, working for kings in what is now Nigeria. Posts like this held up palace verandas and showed royal power. The figures are carved so they seem to step free of the post.

title: Boy on a Ram
why: Goya painted this as a design for a tapestry for the Spanish royal court. It is light and playful, quite unlike the dark visions of his later years. Seeing both sides of Goya shows how war and illness changed his art.

title: Kitchen Scene
why: An early Velázquez, from his years in Seville. A kitchen maid works among pots and food, painted with intense realism. Treating a servant and everyday objects as worthy of art was unusual at the time.

title: The White Tablecloth
why: Chardin found beauty in simple domestic objects: bread, a glass, a white cloth. His quiet still lifes went against the grand fashion of his time. They feel modest and deeply calm.

title: Rocks at the Lighthouse, Biarritz
why: The Spanish painter Sorolla was known as the master of light. He painted outdoors, quickly, catching sun and sea spray. This small seascape shows his fresh, bright touch.

title: Dorothea and Francesca
why: Cecilia Beaux was one of the leading portrait painters in America and the first woman to teach full time at the Pennsylvania Academy. Two girls practise a dance step together. The flowing white paint gives them grace and movement.

title: The Hammock
why: Tissot moved from Paris to London and painted fashionable life. A woman reads in a hammock in a garden in St John's Wood. Many of his London pictures show the same woman, Kathleen Newton, his companion.

title: Distant View of Niagara Falls
why: Thomas Cole founded the Hudson River School, the first American landscape movement. He painted the falls as a sublime wilderness, with tiny figures in the foreground. Even then he worried about industry spoiling such places.

title: Love of Winter
why: Bellows painted people skating in a park in a burst of bright colour. He was associated with the Ashcan School, which painted real urban life. This is one of his more joyful scenes.

title: Portrait of a Princess
why: Mughal painting flourished at the courts of northern India, mixing Persian, Indian and sometimes European styles. Portraits like this were made with fine brushes, sometimes of a single hair. The detail of jewels and fabric was part of the message of status.

title: The Crucifixion
why: Zurbarán painted this for a monastery in Seville. Christ appears against a dark background, almost like a sculpture lit by a single source. It was designed to help monks meditate, and the stillness is the point.

title: The Banks of the Marne in Winter
why: An early Pissarro, painted before Impressionism had a name. The bare trees and grey sky are plain and honest. Pissarro later became a mentor to Cézanne and Gauguin and the only artist to show in all eight Impressionist exhibitions.

title: Still Life with Geranium
why: Matisse painted this as he was developing Fauvism, a style built on bold, unnatural colour. Objects matter less than how the colours sit together. He wanted art to feel like a good armchair: restful and balancing.

title: Mahana no atua (Day of the God)
why: Painted in Paris from memories of Tahiti, this shows a dreamlike scene of worship with flat, decorative colour. It is less a record than an invented world. It is worth enjoying the colour and questioning the fantasy at the same time.

title: Flower Clouds
why: Redon spent years making dark charcoal drawings of dreams, then turned to glowing colour later in life. Here a boat floats under cloud-like flowers. It belongs to Symbolism, which cared more about imagination than observation.
